title: The Tape and the Wario Files
subtitle: The archivist has already read what the tape says; this is the reading of where it came from, which nobody has asked about and which he now cannot stop asking about
filed: Filed after the line-by-line reading, late, once the obvious question had finished not going away
summary: I have written at length about what is on this tape and I stand behind all of it. This page is about the part I skipped: a private argument between two brothers was recorded by somebody, reached the archive through a man who sells things, and has no origin at all. Nobody has asked. I am asking.
thesis:
The cassette is on the desk in front of me, squared to the blotter, spine label blank. I have played it more times than is good for me and I have already filed the line-by-line reading — the one where I argue the fight is not about betrayal but about being seen. I do not withdraw a word of that.

But here is what has kept me at this desk since: **I built that entire argument on an object with no beginning.**

The tape enters the archive already in Wario's possession. Before Wario there is nothing. No recordist, no room, no instruction, no chain. And then — after I had published my reading of the poor copy — a materially cleaner dub surfaced, source unstated, and I amended my filing like a good auditor and did not once ask who had been sitting on the better one.

That omission is mine. This page is the correction.

sections.heading: A Two-Voice Argument Does Not Record Itself
sections.sourceAnchor: A primary source at last — the brothers' argument, in their own voices.
sections.body:
Put your hand on the physical object for a moment, the way I have mine now. It is a tape. Tapes require a machine. Machines require a person to start them, and — this is the part that should have bothered me a year ago — a person to **place** them.

The recording is clean enough that I built a line-by-line reading on it. I distinguished tone. I heard where Mario answers the wrong question. That is not what a device forgotten in a drawer across a room produces; that is a capture from somewhere near the conversation.

So: somebody chose a room, chose a moment, and chose a placement, for a private argument between two brothers.

I can think of three people it might have been and I am going to name none of them, because naming suspects in an archive is how an archive becomes a rumour. What I will commit to is the structural claim: **the most important document in the Mario file was created by a deliberate act, and the actor is not in the file.**

Every conclusion I have drawn about that argument sits on top of that absence. Including the conclusions I like.

sections.heading: The Better Copy Arrived After I Published, And That Is Information
sections.sourceAnchor: Revised same week, once a cleaner dub of the tape surfaced and I heard how much I had missed the first time.
sections.body:
I wrote, in my own filing, that an auditor who does not correct his own work is not an auditor but a fan. I meant it and I acted on it.

What I did not do — and it is the kind of omission I would prosecute in anybody else — is note what the arrival of a second, better copy *implies*.

It implies **copies exist**. It implies somebody made them. And it implies somebody decided when this archive would receive the good one, which was: after reading what I concluded from the bad one.

Now, I can hear the reasonable objection, and it is mine as much as anyone's: dubs surface for extremely dull reasons all the time. Somebody finds a box. A better machine turns up. An archive that reads intent into every delivery will eventually read intent into a postal delay, and I have mocked people for less.

But the dull explanation requires a coincidence — that the improved copy happened to appear in the same week that a widely-read reading of the inferior copy was published. I am not able to make that coincidence feel small.

So I record it as a live possibility rather than a finding: the disclosure may have been **responsive rather than cooperative.** Somebody may be reading what I file and adjusting what I get.

sections.heading: The Custodian Is A Man Whose Entire Method Is Transaction
sections.sourceAnchor: Held by Wario, prior to disclosure.
sections.body:
I am about to be accused of family bias, so let me get in front of it: Wario is not a liar. He is something much more useful to an investigator and much worse for a chain of custody — he is a **dealer**. Things come into his possession and things leave it, and the governing question is always price rather than truth.

That matters here in a specific way. A dealer does not need to forge anything to distort a record. He simply needs to decide *when* to produce a genuine object, and to whom, and in what condition. Every one of those decisions is a thumb on the archive's scale, and none of them is a lie.

He produced a real tape. The tape is authentic — I have staked my reading on it and I stake it again here. But an authentic object released at a chosen moment by a man who trades in leverage is not the same thing as evidence freely given, and the archive has been treating it as though it were.

I notice, too, that nobody asked him. Not in the filing, not in the sessions around it, not by me. A man handed us the single most consequential document in the Mario disappearance and the entire company's follow-up question was *play it again*.

I have played it again. Six times, by the curtains-drawn count in the filing. It is time somebody asked him where he got it.

sections.heading: I Have Played It Six Times And The Sixth Taught Me Nothing New
sections.sourceAnchor: Midnight, second day, sixth rewind. The curtains have not been opened since the clinic.
sections.body:
The filing's own image is a man in a chair at midnight on the second day, sixth rewind, curtains still shut since the clinic. I recognise the posture because I am currently in it.

And I want to put something uncomfortable in writing, because this page is supposed to be where I am honest rather than merely correct.

**The sixth rewind taught me nothing the third had not already.** By then I was not listening for information. I was listening because the voices were there and the room was quiet and stopping the tape meant going back to a file where Mario is still missing. That is not research. That is company.

I raise it because it bears directly on the provenance question. A document you have played six times stops being a document. It becomes furniture — a thing so familiar that asking where it came from feels like an insult to an old friend. That is precisely how an archive ends up building two filings on an unexamined gift: not through carelessness, but through **intimacy**. You do not interrogate the chain of custody of something you can recite.

So take this section as a methodological confession attached to a case note. The reason nobody asked Wario where he got the tape is that by the time anybody thought to, the tape no longer felt like evidence. It felt like ours.

It is not ours. Somebody made it, somebody kept it, and somebody chose the hour we heard it clearly.

sections.heading: None Of This Weakens The Reading, And I Will Not Let It Be Used That Way
sections.sourceAnchor: Read line by line, the fight is not about Mario at all.
sections.body:
I want a firewall here, because I know how provenance arguments get misused and I have no intention of handing anybody that tool.

Questioning where a document came from is **not** the same as questioning whether it is true. The tape's content is corroborated by its own internal texture — two voices that know each other's history, a fight with the specific ugly shape that only real fights have, and a line of Luigi's that no forger inventing a corruption story would have thought to include because it does not serve one.

My line-by-line reading stands. Luigi is not asking to be forgiven; he is asking to be **acknowledged**, and Mario keeps answering a question nobody asked. I believed that when I had the poor dub and I believe it more with the clean one.

So let the record be exact about what this page claims and what it does not. It does not claim the tape is doctored. It does not claim the argument went differently. It claims one narrow thing: **we do not know who wanted us to hear this, and that is a fact about the case which is currently recorded nowhere.**

An unknown benefactor is still an unknown. Two filings of conclusions rest on a gift, and nobody has looked the gift in the mouth.

verdict:
**The tape is true and its provenance is a hole, and the archive has been treating the first fact as though it settles the second.** It does not.

I stand fully behind my line-by-line reading. The argument is about being seen, Mario loses it by answering the wrong question, and the impostor-derived versions the archive carried for two filings were wrong. None of that is in question here, and I will not have this page cited by anyone trying to reopen it.

What I am filing is a gap. Somebody deliberately recorded a private argument between two brothers. Somebody made copies. Somebody handed one to a dealer, or the dealer was there himself, and somebody chose to release a cleaner version only after reading what I had concluded from the worse one. Not a single link in that chain is documented, and I built two filings on top of it without once writing the words *where did this come from*.

My recommendation is the plainest in this archive: **ask Wario.** He is available, he is not hostile, and nobody has put the question to him. Then establish who produced the second dub and when it was made, because a copy has a date and a date has a person attached to it.

Until then I am attaching a standing caution to my own best work: every conclusion in the Mario file currently rests on a gift from an unidentified giver. WAH.

researchDesk.title: Waluigi's After-Hours Research Desk
researchDesk.intro: Two optional checks, run after the verdict as the form requires. One d6 each, filed once. Each returns a supplemental inference of mine or the precise point at which I stop being able to argue.

rolls.title: What does the audio quality say about where the machine sat?
rolls.prompt: Consider that the capture is clean enough to support tone analysis of two distinct speakers throughout a moving argument, and ask what that requires of the recorder's position.
rolls.success: Inference only: a capture that holds both voices intelligibly through a mobile argument implies a machine placed centrally and deliberately rather than one running by chance in a corner, which narrows the recordist to someone with prior access to that room.
rolls.failure: Honest limit. I am an auditor, not an engineer, and the surviving copy has been dubbed at least once — which means the qualities I would reason from may belong to the copying rather than the original.

rolls.title: Was the cleaner dub released in response to my filing?
rolls.prompt: Place the publication date of my first line-by-line reading against the week the improved copy surfaced, and ask whether the sequence supports a responsive disclosure.
rolls.success: Supplemental inference: the improved copy appearing only after a widely-read reading of the inferior one is consistent with somebody monitoring this archive's output and metering what it receives — which would make the holder an active party rather than a source.
rolls.failure: This is where I stop. Two events in one week is a sequence, not a mechanism, and I have publicly mocked people for building conspiracies out of exactly this much.
